```{python}
SPACK_YAML_PATH = PROJECT_DIR / "spack.yaml"
SPACK_EXTRAS = {}

import os
n_cores = len(os.sched_getaffinity(0)) or 1
```

We keep environment definitions in Python dictionaries so we 
can inspect and mutate them in the notebook before writing files. 
One of the most important environment definitions is `spack.yaml`, 
which defines the Spack environment for this project. Why `spack`?

While `conda` is a popular package manager for data science, it is not
it's actually not a great fit for HPC environments. In my experience,
it fails to make obvious choices about low level system libraries —
or at least, it does not make it obvious _to me_ what they are
and how to fix them. Spack, on the other hand, has an API, ecosystem,
and documentation workflow that kinda leans into the differences of HPC.
One of those differences being the multi-user nature,
where users do not have root access to the system, and therefore cannot
install system libraries.

Think, for example, of the last time you installed a very serious, high
complexity and volume package — something like `sf` or `torch`.
You likely had to install a low-level system library first, and then install the package.
With `conda`, you _might_ find the installation works, from the top
to the bottom, without problems, but if it fails, you don't often get a
lot of help in figuring out what the missing pieces are _underneath_ the
package you care about — for e.g., geospatial work with `sf` requires
a harmonious installation of `gdal`, `proj`, and `geos`, which are 
all low-level system libraries that must be installed first. On your
personal laptop, you might install these once and never think about
them again, but on an HPC, you either have to figure out how to install
a system library without root access, or you have to dance around
paths and environment variables all afternoon until it works,
and start all over again the next time you inevitably need
to do some geospatial work again in a different folder.

Spack, on the other hand, has a more explicit dependency graph 
and can help you figure out what is missing and how to install it.
Or, again, at least, it is more explicit about what is missing and how to install it.
I'm not saying you can't do all of your environment management with
`conda`, but I am saying that my turnover time for figuring out what is missing and how to install it is much faster with `spack` than with `conda`.

That being said, the `spack` environment file is a YAML file,
and we can set that up with a dictionary. For this layer,
I recommend installing a minimal Spack environment that ONLY
installs the languages required for doing science, — not installing
the languages' libraries. Spack is not perfect and is not
designed for managing libraries _for_ the language. Instead,
we'll define language libraries in the next section.

For now, here is a minimal `spack` `spec` with the stuff I usually see:

```{python}
spack_env = {
    "spack": {
        "specs": [
            "r@4.4.3",
            "python@3.14",
            "libiconv",
            "ncurses",
            "openblas",
            "curl",
            "openssl",
            "pkgconf",
            "abseil-cpp",
            "zlib-ng",
            "proj@9.4.1",
            "gdal@3.9.3~arrow",
            "geos",
            "gmake",
            "cmake",
            "libgit2"
            
        ],

        "view": "/work/.spack-env/view",

        "config": {
            "install_tree": {
                "root": "/work/.spack-env/install"
                },
            "source_cache": "/work/.spack/cache/source",
            "misc_cache": "/work/.spack/cache/misc",
            "build_stage": ["/work/.spack/stage"]
            },
        },
    }
```

You can change the exact version of the language using the `@` syntax,
and to see a complete list of what packages are registered in the
`spack` package index, you can run `spack list` and `grep` that,
or go to the [Spack package index](https://packages.spack.io/).

Write helpers:

```{python}
def write_spack_yaml():
    SPACK_YAML_PATH.write_text(yaml.safe_dump(spack_env, sort_keys=False))
```

```{python}
#| eval: false
write_spack_yaml()
```

Try the first basic install; we'll need to create our container directories while we're at it:

```{python}
show_spython(
    spython_exec(
        f"""
        export SPACK_DISABLE_LOCAL_CONFIG=true
        mkdir -p /work /tmp/spack-user-config /tmp/spack-user-cache /tmp/spack-misc-cache

        . /opt/spack/share/spack/setup-env.sh
        cd /work
        spack env activate --create -d .
        spack concretize
        spack install --deprecated --fail-fast -j{n_cores} --no-checksum
        """,
        image=str(TMP_SANDBOX),
        writable=True,
        bind_project=True,
    )
)
```

If this fails, modify `spack_env` in Python, write it again, and retry.

Example:

```{python}
#| eval: false
spack_env["spack"]["specs"].append("libgit2")
write_spack_yaml()
```

We also define a list of environment variables that our `spack` environment
will typically require in this list:

```{python}
SPACK_EXTRAS["env_vars"] = [
    "SPACK_DISABLE_LOCAL_CONFIG=true",
    "SPACK_USER_CONFIG_PATH=/tmp/spack-user-config",
    "SPACK_USER_CACHE_PATH=/tmp/spack-user-cache",
    "SPACK_MISC_CACHE_PATH=/tmp/spack-misc-cache",
    "LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/work/.spack-env/view/lib:/work/.spack-env/view/lib64:${LD_LIBRARY_PATH:-}"
]
```

Our runtime will require installation and activation of the `spack` environment
each time it is used.
We'll keep these in a list of commands that can be added to the
launch script:

```{python}
runtime_commands = [
    "export SPACK_DISABLE_LOCAL_CONFIG=true",
    ". /opt/spack/share/spack/setup-env.sh",
    "cd /work",
    "spack env activate -d .",
    "spack concretize",
    f"spack install --deprecated --fail-fast -j{n_cores} --no-checksum"
]
SPACK_EXTRAS["runtime_commands"] = runtime_commands
```
